problem: "a few microvolts between the inputs is enough to slam the output against a supply rail" understates the real number by roughly twenty times. With AOL = 10⁵ and ±12 V supplies the input must reach about 110 µV (55 µV of overdrive) before the output clamps, and the chapter's own worked example uses exactly this figure.
fix: "a few tens of microvolts between the inputs is enough to slam the output against a supply rail"

problem: The acronym "IOA (ideal op-amp) model)" is not a standard textbook name; presenting it as something "some syllabi call" the circuit is an invented term and may confuse a student who searches for it.
fix: Delete the sentence, or write: "The resulting model is simply called the ideal op-amp model."

where: Section 2, paragraph after the strip-width formula
problem: "A differential input of one millivolt is twenty times too big" is arithmetically off: 1 mV = 1000 µV against a linear limit of 55 µV gives about 18 times, not 20. Against the full 110 µV strip it is about 9 times, so the comparison base is also ambiguous.
fix: "A differential input of one millivolt is about eighteen times the 55 µV limit, so the output is driven hard into saturation."

problem: The open-loop gain appears as plain text "AOL" in the formula line while everywhere else it is written A<sub>OL</sub> (and once as "A_OL" in the figure). Inconsistent notation for the same symbol.
fix: Use A<sub>OL</sub> consistently in the formula line, the figure note and the surrounding prose.
